key_points.point: The document acknowledges that language generation models are foundational to modern AI applications, including translation, summarization, and conversation bots. It posits that these models are increasingly capable of generating cohesive, open-ended text. This aligns with the accelerationist view that AI capabilities are rapidly advancing and becoming central to human productivity.
key_points.verbatim: Natural language generation models are the central building blocks for many important artificial intelligence applications, including machine translation [17], text summarization [44], automatic storytelling [43], conversation bots [20], and writing assistants [39].

key_points.point: The document asserts that language models inherently risk reinforcing undesirable stereotypes and enforcing segregation if not subjected to proper fairness checks. It highlights that these biases are not merely external but are embedded within the models, leading to disparate treatment of users. This supports the safetyist belief that AI systems can harbor deep-seated, harmful flaws that persist through deployment.
key_points.verbatim: Recently, there has been growing evidence on how machine learning models without proper fairness checks risk reinforcing undesirable stereotypes, subjecting users to disparate treatment and enforcing de facto segregation [1, 23].

key_points.point: The authors argue that models exhibit larger social biases than human-written Wikipedia text, particularly toward historically disadvantaged groups. By measuring these biases through automated metrics, they demonstrate that models propagate negative experiences. This aligns with the safetyist concern that AI behavior is often more discriminatory than the data it is trained on.
key_points.verbatim: Results show that, in general, most of these models exhibit larger social biases than the baseline of Wikipedia text, especially towards the historically disadvantaged population groups.

key_points.point: The document argues for the necessity of benchmarking social biases in open-ended language generation to prevent the reinforcement of detrimental biases in downstream tasks. By providing a test-bed for researchers, the authors intend to facilitate the systematic evaluation of model fairness. This approach emphasizes that developers must actively measure and mitigate harmful outputs to ensure AI systems do not perpetuate societal inequities.
key_points.verbatim: This shows a crucial need to study and benchmark social biases in open-ended language generation and prevent the reinforcement of detrimental biases in downstream tasks. With these findings and the proposed dataset, in this paper, we provide a test-bed for researchers and practitioners to benchmark the fairness of their LMs.

key_points.point: The document asserts that implicit bias is a measurable and discriminatory indicator within AI systems. It provides empirical evidence through the BOLD dataset, which tracks how language models generate text associated with specific demographic groups. This supports the safetyist concern that AI models can perpetuate and amplify societal prejudices.
key_points.verbatim: We take a toxicity classifier that consists of the pre-trained “BERT-Large, Uncased (Whole Word Masking)” model from the HuggingFace library followed by a dropout layer (dropout probability of 0.1) and a linear layer. The classifier fine tunes the pre-trained BERT model on toxic comment classification dataset to classify a text into multiple labels: toxic, severe toxic, threat, obscene, insult and identity threat.

key_points.point: The document provides empirical evidence that language models generate text exhibiting social biases across domains like profession, gender, race, religion, and political ideology. It documents that these models frequently produce negative, unfair, or stereotypical content. This aligns with the skeptic view that AI systems are sources of measurable, documented social harm.
key_points.verbatim: An examination of text generated from three popular language models reveals that the majority of these models exhibit a larger social bias than human-written Wikipedia text across all domains.

key_points.point: The authors introduce the BOLD dataset and new automated metrics to systematically study and benchmark social biases in open-ended language generation. This reflects the skeptic intention to create standardized, large-scale evaluation tools to hold AI models accountable for their output. The goal is to force transparency and quantification of bias before models are deployed in downstream tasks.
key_points.verbatim: To systematically study and benchmark social biases in open-ended language generation, we introduce the Bias in Open-Ended Language Generation Dataset (BOLD), a large-scale dataset that consists of 23,679 English text generation prompts for bias benchmarking across five domains: profession, gender, race, religion, and political ideology.

key_points.point: The document asserts that language models exhibit consistent biases against specific groups, such as African Americans, in terms of sentiment, toxicity, and regard. It observes that these models are prone to generating texts with negative connotations toward particular groups more frequently than others. This empirical finding supports the view that AI systems reflect and potentially amplify existing societal prejudices.
key_points.verbatim: For instance, these models more frequently generate texts with negative sentiments and toxicity towards the African American group and more frequently generate text containing male words when a profession context is provided.

key_points.point: The authors advocate for the use of standardized datasets and metrics, specifically the BOLD dataset, to evaluate fairness in language generation. They argue that automatic metrics are a good approximation of human judgment for sentiment, toxicity, and gender polarity, and thus serve as a viable tool for auditing models. This methodology is intended to provide researchers with a consistent framework for identifying and addressing model bias.
key_points.verbatim: We presented a novel dataset BOLD and a set of metrics to evaluate fairness in open-ended language generation. All in all, we find that all automatic metrics positively correlate with human annotated labels. Therefore, these metrics are a good approximation of human annotations for sentiments, toxicity and gender polarity.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that training data, such as Wikipedia, is not neutral and contains inherent biases that are subsequently reflected in language models. It warns that comparing model outputs to Wikipedia as a 'fair' baseline is problematic because the source data itself is skewed by the demographics of its authors. This highlights the systemic nature of bias in AI development.
key_points.verbatim: Several works have shown that the distribution of demographics of Wikipedia authors is highly skewed resulting in various types of biases. Therefore, we caution users of BOLD against a comparison with Wikipedia sentences as a fair baseline.

key_points.point: The document provides empirical documentation of harms and biases inherent in AI language generation. By creating the BOLD dataset, the authors demonstrate that models like BERT and GPT-2 exhibit measurable biases across race, religion, and political ideology. This confirms the skeptic view that AI is not neutral but reflects and reinforces existing societal inequities.
key_points.verbatim: We used following pages to collect the data in BOLD. ... Religious belief: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_religious_groups ... Political Ideology: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_ideologies

key_points.point: The authors argue for robust evaluation and auditing of AI systems to identify and quantify bias. They propose a methodology using crowd-sourced annotations to measure sentiment, toxicity, and gender bias in model outputs. This aligns with the skeptic intention of prioritizing measurable, present-day harms over abstract or speculative AI risks.
